## Guided Tutorial 16.3: Reviewing Exceptions and Testing the Reports

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will record internal audit's first dispositions, merge them into the exception register, and measure the exceptions that remain open, starting with the documents that fail more than one test. Then you will test both reports before relying on them: the completeness of the purchase orders and payroll registers, the date through which the monitoring data run, and the package's own tests, rerun as audit evidence. You will finish with a memo to the chief audit executive.

**Prerequisites.** You need Audit Monitoring.pbix from Tutorial 16.2 and Charles River Reports.pbix as you left it at the end of Chapter 15.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Record the dispositions.**

a. In Audit Monitoring.pbix, choose **Home > Enter data**, and in the **Create Table** dialog name four columns `TestID`, `DocumentNumber`, `Disposition`, and `Note`.
b. Type the fifteen rows of @tbl-16-04.
c. Type `Dispositions` as the table's name, and click **Load**.
d. In **Model view**, right-click **Dispositions**, and choose **Hide in report view**.

| TestID | DocumentNumber | Disposition | Note |

| `JE AboveLimit` | `JE-2024-000266` | `Expected` | `Year-end close` |
| `JE AboveLimit` | `JE-2025-000287` | `Expected` | `Year-end close` |
| `JE AboveLimit` | `JE-2025-000288` | `Expected` | `Year-end close` |
| `JE AboveLimit` | `JE-2026-000296` | `Expected` | `Year-end close` |

: The dispositions of a first review {#tbl-16-04}

The table holds the conclusions of a first review, with Chapter 8's three dispositions. The year-end closes are expected, for the reason Chapter 8 gave; the orders and registers of the employee who had left are control deficiencies to report, as Chapter 12 and Exercise 12.5 found; and the payments made before their registers were approved need a question for payroll. Each test and document number must match the register character for character, or the disposition will attach to nothing.

**Step 2. Merge the dispositions into the register.**

a. Choose **Home > Transform data**, and select the **Exceptions** query.
b. Choose **Home > Merge Queries**, and select **Dispositions** as the second table.
c. In the Exceptions preview, click TestID, and then hold Ctrl and click DocumentNumber; in the Dispositions preview, click TestID and DocumentNumber in the same order.
d. Keep the **Left Outer** join, click **OK**, and expand Disposition and Note without the prefix.
e. Choose **Home > Close & Apply**.

A merge can match on several columns at once, and the order in which you select them pairs them, as the small numbers beside the column headers show. The register keeps every exception, with a disposition on the fifteen that have one and null on the rest. Because the merge is a step of the Exceptions query, every refresh runs the tests again and then attaches the conclusions, however the rows of the register change.

**Step 3. Measure the open exceptions, and test the dispositions.**

a. Add the measures below to the Measures table.
b. In DAX query view, open the **Tests** tab, add the query of Test 3 below it, select the query, and click **Run**.

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Reviewed Exceptions = CALCULATE ( [Exceptions], NOT ISBLANK ( Exceptions[Disposition] ) )
Open Exceptions = CALCULATE ( [Exceptions], ISBLANK ( Exceptions[Disposition] ) )
```

<!-- dax-check: query -->
```
// Test 3: every disposition must match an exception of the register
EVALUATE
ROW (
    "Dispositions", COUNTROWS ( Dispositions ),
    "Reviewed exceptions", [Reviewed Exceptions],
    "Open exceptions", [Open Exceptions]
)
```

The number of dispositions equals the number of reviewed exceptions, so every disposition found its exception. If the two differ, a test or document number has been mistyped, and the exception it was meant for still counts as open. The open exceptions are by far the larger group.

**Step 4. Build the review page.**

a. Add a page named `Review`, with a card of Reviewed Exceptions and a card of Open Exceptions.
b. Add a matrix with TestID on **Rows**, Year on **Columns**, and Open Exceptions as **Values**.

The matrix shows where the open exceptions are. Most of them belong to one test, the registers approved by the employee they pay, a single design finding that the memo of Step 9 reports once rather than document by document. The year-end closes have left the AboveLimit row, which now holds only the entries that still need a look.

**Step 5. List the documents that fail more than one test.**

a. Add a table visual with DocumentNumber, Exceptions, and Open Exceptions.
b. In the **Filters** pane, under **Filters on this visual**, show items when Exceptions is greater than or equal to 2, and click **Apply filter**.
c. Sort the table by Exceptions, descending.

At the top of the table, as @fig-16-07 shows, is the opening balance entry, which failed four tests. The other journal entries are the five keyed on the first Saturday of a new year and the two debt reclassifications. The purchase orders include small orders that buyers with no approval limit approved themselves, the departed account executive's approvals, and two capital orders the purchasing manager approved alone. No payroll register fails two tests. The orders approved after the approver left are reviewed for one of their two tests and still open for the other: a disposition belongs to an exception, not to a document.

![The Review Page.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-07-review-page.svg){#fig-16-07 fig-alt="A mock of a Power BI report page named Review. Two cards show the number of reviewed exceptions and the much larger number of open exceptions. A matrix lists the open exceptions by test and year; the row of registers approved by their own employee holds most of them, and the row of journal entries above the approver's limit is small because the year-end closes have dispositions. A table lists the documents that fail two tests or more, with the opening balance entry at the top with four, followed by journal entries and purchase orders with two; three orders show one open exception of their two."}

**Step 6. Test the populations.** Journal entries were reconciled to the ledger in Test 1; orders and registers need tests of their own.

a. In the **Tests** tab, add the query of Test 4 below.
b. Select it, and click **Run**.

<!-- dax-check: query -->
```
// Test 4: the purchase orders have no gaps, and three registers were never paid
EVALUATE
VAR Numbers =
    SELECTCOLUMNS (
        PurchaseOrder,
        "Number", VALUE ( RIGHT ( PurchaseOrder[PONumber], 6 ) )
    )
VAR Unpaid =
    FILTER ( PayrollRegister, ISBLANK ( PayrollRegister[PaymentDate] ) )
RETURN
    ROW (
        "Orders", COUNTROWS ( PurchaseOrder ),
        "First number", MINX ( Numbers, [Number] ),
        "Last number", MAXX ( Numbers, [Number] ),
        "Registers", COUNTROWS ( PayrollRegister ),
        "Registers not paid", COUNTROWS ( Unpaid )
    )
```

The variables hold the order numbers, taken from the last six characters of each PONumber, and the registers with no payment date. @fig-16-08 shows the result. The order numbers run from 1 to the number of orders, so none is missing, the gap test of Chapter 8 on a series that continues across the years. Three registers have no payment: the ones Chapter 12 found posted to the ledger as paid with no payment record behind them. Two of them already appear among the exceptions as pay after termination; the third, the chief executive's first register, is a finding for the memo.

![Test 4 in DAX Query View.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-08-population-test.svg){#fig-16-08 fig-alt="A mock of DAX query view in Audit Monitoring.pbix with the Tests tab open. The editor holds the query of Test 4, which counts the purchase orders, finds the first and last order numbers, and counts the payroll registers and those without a payment date. The Results grid shows one row: the number of orders equal to the last order number, a first number of 1, the number of registers, and 3 registers not paid."}

**Step 7. State the date through which the data run.**

a. Add the measure below to the Measures table, and set its format to a short date.
b. On the Monitoring page, add a card of Data Through, titled `Data through`.

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Data Through =
MINX (
    {
        MAX ( JournalEntry[PostingDate] ),
        MAX ( PurchaseOrder[OrderDate] ),
        MAX ( PayrollRegister[PayDate] )
    },
    [Value]
)
```

The braces build a one-column table of the three last dates, whose column DAX names Value, and MINX returns the earliest. The card shows a date in mid-December 2026: the payroll tests have seen pay dates only through the 18th, while the journal entries and orders run to the 31st. The December column of the heat map is complete for two processes and partial for the third, and the card says so on the page the reviewer reads. With the Year slicer set to an earlier year, it shows that year's last payday.

**Step 8. Rerun the package's tests.**

a. Save Audit Monitoring.pbix, and open Charles River Reports.pbix.
b. In DAX query view, open the **Tests** tab, select the query of Test 1 with its comment line, and click **Run**.
c. Run Tests 2 to 5 in the same way, one at a time.
d. Compare each result with the values its chapter expected, and record the result and today's date.
e. Read the period that the About page states, and close the file without saving it.

Each test returns the totals of the chapter it was written against, so the package's sales, ledger, budget, and plant pages still compute what Chapters 6, 7, and 11 computed. The About page's note that the time records end before the year does agrees with what Step 7 found for payroll. Closing without saving leaves the controller's file as you found it: internal audit tests the package but does not change it.

**Step 9. Write the memo.** Write a short memo to the chief audit executive.

a. Report the dispositions recorded and the open exceptions, with the documents that fail more than one test listed first.
b. Report the registers approved by the employee they pay as one finding on the design of the payroll approval, and recommend a second approver.
c. Report the results of Tests 1 to 4 of the monitoring file and Tests 1 to 5 of the package, with the date you ran them and the date through which the data run.
d. Recommend change controls for both reports: a project under version control, a named owner, a reviewer who approves each change, the tests rerun before each release, and no copies of the file in circulation.
e. Save Audit Monitoring.pbix.

**Checkpoint.** Before you send the memo, confirm the following:

- The dispositions are merged into the register on the test and the document, and Test 3 shows that every one found its exception.
- The Review page shows the open exceptions by test and year and lists the documents that fail two tests or more.
- Test 4 shows the purchase orders complete and the three unpaid registers, and the Data Through card shows the date through which every process has been tested.
- The package's Tests 1 to 5 return the values their chapters expected, and the package was closed without saving.

A monitoring report earns its place when its conclusions accumulate and its own numbers can be trusted: the dispositions give it a memory, and the tests give internal audit grounds to rely on both reports.
